newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan central bank seen facing uphill task.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan central bank seen facing uphill task.

text.p: The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP), soon to get new powers, will need all its extra clout to control monetary policy amid rising government borrowing and low forex reserves, analysts said on Thursday.
The SBP said in a statement that in the next few days the caretaker government would grant it greater strength to regulate the banking system and handle monetary policy.
"These changes give extensive powers to the State Bank for regulation of the banking system," it quoted central bank governor Mohammad Yaqub as telling bankers on Wednesday.
"The autonomy of the State Bank in formulation and implementation of monetary policy has also been substantially enhanced," Yaqub said.
He said the changes would enable the SBP Board of Directors to conduct monetary policy independently, and to determine and regulate money supply and government borrowing from the SBP.
Analysts and bankers welcomed the move but had doubts about the central bank's ability to deal with runaway government borrowing, fragile foreign exchange reserves and bad debts.
"It is a positive development, but the task lying ahead of the central bank is very tough," Maqsood Ahmad, vice president of the private Muslim Commercial Bank, told Reuters.
Curbing government domestic borrowing and boosting reserves would be a difficult job at a time when Pakistan has a daily outflow of $25-30 million in debt and import payments, he said.

The state's National Credit Consultative Council said on Wednesday it had raised the credit target 14.18 percent to 137.1 billion rupees for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from 102 billion in 1995/96 after credit ballooned in the first half.

The SBP said domestic credit had risen 13 percent to 128 billion rupees in the first six months, against a target of 102 billion rupees for the whole year. "Government borrowing for budgetary support alone accounted for well over 60 percent of total credit expansion up to December 26, 1996," it said.
Abid Naqvi, research head at Taurus Securities, linked the decline in reserves, at $1.461 billion on January 2 from $2.405 billion a year ago, to higher domestic government borrowing.
"While the latter can be partially explained by a higher than targeted deficit, it could possibly also be due to lower than expected foreign borrowing for budgetary support," he said.

He said inflows of resident and non-resident forex deposits, short-term commercial debt, asset sales and foreign direct investment had financed much of the $4.2 billion current budget deficit in fiscal 1995/96.
Ahmad said most foreign lenders and investors were reluctant to put money into Pakistan, where a general election is due on February 3, given its present political and economic woes.
The caretaker government, with more than two-thirds of its allotted life-span over, is trying to clinch a World Bank loan to back banking sector reform, one of its economic priorities.

Yaqub said the government was formulating new laws on foreclosure and banking tribunals to speed up the process of recovery of bad debts; the merger and consolidation of various state-run financial institutions; and setting up a Resolution Trust Corporation to dispose of their non-performing portfolios.

But a foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said most of the bad loan portfolio in the banking system was held by state-owned banks and financial institutions. Most of the big loan defaulters were politicians or had political backing.
"How far the new powers are going to help the central bank counter the political clout of the defaulters is yet to be seen," the banker said.
